Repay
rē-pā´
v. (to pay back; to requite; rendering Hebrew shalam, Greek antapodidomi, apodidomi, and apotino)
Old French repaier, to pay back. The Hebrew shalam is to make whole or complete — the same root as shalom: a debt repaid is a peace restored.

Biblical Definition

“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19). The Samaritan to the host: “Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee” (Luk 10:35). Paul for Onesimus: “If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account; I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it” (Phm 1:18–19). God of Himself: “Who hath prevented me, that I should repay him? whatsoever is under the whole heaven is mine” (Job 41:11). “According to their deeds, accordingly he will repay, fury to his adversaries” (Isa 59:18). He “repayeth them that hate him to their face” (Deu 7:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines repay as to pay back; to refund; to make return or requital; to recompense, in a good or bad sense.

expand to see more

REPAY, v.t. To pay back; to refund; as, to repay money borrowed.

2. To make return or requital; in a good or bad sense; as, to repay kindness; to repay an injury.

3. To recompense; to compensate.

Key Scripture

Rom 12:19 — "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."

Luk 10:35 — "And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee."

Phm 1:19 — "I Paul have written it with mine own hand, I will repay it: albeit I do not say to thee how thou owest unto me even thine own self besides."

Job 41:11 — "Who hath prevented me, that I should repay him? whatsoever is under the whole heaven is mine."

Isa 59:18 — "According to their deeds, accordingly he will repay, fury to his adversaries, recompence to his enemies; to the islands he will repay recompence."

Modern Corruption

Man takes vengeance because he doubts God will repay, and God asks who ever lent Him anything.

expand to see more

Romans 12:19 forbids vengeance by promising it. The Christian gives place unto wrath — steps aside and leaves room for it — not because the wrong does not matter but because Someone has said I will repay, and He keeps better accounts. Every act of private revenge is a vote of no confidence in that sentence. Job 41:11 is the sentence from the other direction, quoted by Paul at the end of Romans 11: who hath prevented me, that I should repay him? — who has ever put God in his debt? The prosperity gospel runs on the answer that we have, that a gift given obliges God to repay with interest, and God's own words in Job are that everything under heaven is already His. Philemon 19 is the gospel's use of the word: Paul putting a runaway's debt on his own account and signing for it. It is the picture of imputation drawn by the man who taught the doctrine.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shalam (H7999), to make whole, repay, requite; Greek antapodidomi (G467), to repay, requite; apodidomi (G591), to pay back; apotino (G661), to pay off.

expand to see more

Hebrew shalam, piel (H7999) — to repay, requite; Deuteronomy 7:10, Job 21:31, 41:11, Isaiah 59:18, Psalm 37:21.

Greek antapodidomi (G467) — to repay, recompense; Romans 12:19, Hebrews 10:30; apodidomi (G591), Luke 10:35; apotino (G661), Philemon 1:19.

Usage

"“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” — vengeance forbidden by being promised."

"“Who hath prevented me, that I should repay him?” — no one has lent God anything."

"“Put that on mine account… I will repay it” — imputation, signed by Paul."
